subtasks.name: Receive and read referral letters
subtasks.description: Incoming referral letters are received and read by intake staff. The AI would read each letter and prepare it for the steps that follow.
subtasks.rationale: Routine intake of documents. Errors are likely to be caught in later checks, but they cause delay and rework. Many referrals arrive, and each is about a patient.

subtasks.name: Extract referral details
subtasks.description: The AI pulls key details from the letter, such as patient identifiers, the referring provider, the reason for referral, the history and the listed tests.
subtasks.rationale: Structured data capture that follows clear steps. Errors can mislead later steps, but the clinician checks them before the decision. Runs for every referral.

subtasks.name: Check required tests and history are attached
subtasks.description: Compare the referral against the clinic's list of required tests and history. Flag what is missing so it can be requested from the referrer.
subtasks.rationale: Follows a checklist, but some items may be judged relevant or not. A missed gap or a false flag can change the urgency category and delay care.

subtasks.name: Suggest an urgency category with reasons
subtasks.description: The AI proposes an urgency category for the referral and lists its reasons. Today a nurse places the referral in a category.
subtasks.rationale: Weighs competing clinical factors that experienced people could judge differently. A category set too low could delay care and harm a patient's health. It directly shapes the priority decision.

subtasks.name: Draft a summary for the triage clinician
subtasks.description: The AI writes a one-paragraph summary of the referral, the missing information and the suggested category for the clinician to read.
subtasks.rationale: The clinician may rely on the summary in place of the full letter. An omission or distortion could change the decision. Deciding what to include takes clinical sense.

subtasks.name: Confirm urgency category and book the patient
subtasks.description: The triage clinician reviews the referral and the AI's suggestion, confirms or changes the category, and the patient is booked.
subtasks.rationale: This is the final clinical decision about priority and access to care. It relies on experience and has serious consequences for the patient's health if it is wrong.

assumptions: The clinic has a written list of required tests and history for each type of referral.
Referral letters arrive as text, scanned documents or faxes that the AI can read.
Missing information is requested from the referrer by clinic staff, not by the AI.
The triage clinician sees the original letter as well as the AI summary.
The clinic uses a fixed set of urgency categories.
clarifyingQuestions: Does the triage clinician read the full referral letter, or mainly the AI summary?
Who requests missing information from the referrer, and how is it tracked?
Do some urgent referrals, such as suspected cancer, follow a separate fast-track process?

narrative.executiveSummary: The verdict is go with conditions, and the AIA-inspired indicative tier is III. BC FIPPA applies, so the team should consider a privacy impact assessment with reasonable security and a supplementary assessment for storage or processing outside Canada, while the Health Canada medical device rules likely trigger a classification check. The privacy office is the likely owner of the FIPPA work, and the clinical lead, with the vendor's regulatory affairs, is the likely owner of the classification check.
narrative.splitNarrative: AI does it (spot-checked) for Receive and read referral letters and Extract referral details. AI drafts, a person checks and signs off for Check required tests and history are attached and Draft a summary for the triage clinician. A person does it (AI may assist) for Suggest an urgency category with reasons and Confirm urgency category and book the patient. This is a starting split that the team will move as evidence comes in. The next split review is on 2026-12-26, and reviews are monthly.
leverNarratives: Let the team that does the work decide which steps the AI does, and change that over time, using tools and labels shared with other teams. Keep the guardrail Shared platform in place. The direct cost is some automation efficiency, because you give up part of the consistency and scale of one split shared by all teams.

Let the team adjust the split as it learns, on top of a fixed base of data formats, hand-off points and escalation thresholds, and re-check it monthly. Keep the guardrail Standardized base in place. The direct cost is some automation efficiency, as the team spends attention adjusting and outputs vary more above the base.

Hold a weekly joint working session between the AI team and the operating unit. Keep the guardrail Retained differentiation in place, with dedicated time for technical and for domain work. The direct cost is some standalone depth on each side, as experts and AI specialists spend time on each other's work.
narrative.rolloutNarrative: Days 1–30, Foundation & guardrails: complete the privacy and classification work, set up the shared platform and standardized base, and publish the starting split. Days 31–60, Shadow pilot & calibration: run the AI in shadow mode, calibrate escalation thresholds and feed corrections back. Days 61–90, Controlled scale & audit: go live in controlled increments, hold the first split review and audit a sample of decisions. Track median days from referral to triage decision, decision quality on non-routine cases (sampled expert review), and corrections fed back into the system per month.
